newsitem.title: USA: Fed ready to reverse 1995 rate "insurance"-sources.
newsitem.headline: Fed ready to reverse 1995 rate "insurance"-sources.

text.p: The Federal Reserve, though willing to consider that changes in the U.S. economy may have raised the threshhold of non-inflationary trend growth, sees no need to maintain the interest rate insurance it took in 1995 to ensure a lasting expansion, according to Fed sources.

"The goal of monetary policy is to ensure long-term sustainable growth," one Fed source told Reuters, adding the three rate cuts that lowered the federal funds rate from 6.0 percent to 5.25 percent between mid-1995 and January 1996 were aimed at ensuring a lasting expansion.
Gross Domestic Product expanded at a meager 1.3 percent, fourth quarter over fourth quarter, in 1995 and at a 3.1 percent pace in 1996.

The source said the high level of resource utilization, mainly in the labor market and the rapid back-to-back pace of growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 and first quarter of 1997 were evidence "there is no longer a need for such insurance."

The Fed, which last lowered the federal funds rate to 5.25 percent in January 1996, raised it to 5.50 percent on March 25 -- a "prudent" move Fed chairman Alan Greenspan defended in a speech in New York on Thursday.
"The risk, this time, clearly is on the upside, not on the downside," the source added, noting that the Fed does not intend its policy to be reactive to "rear-view mirror" inflation data.

"The concern at the Fed is to implement a policy that does not contribute to inflation and ensures long-term sustainable growth. That's the goal," the source said, adding that long-term market rates have not risen to a level where they would exert an added drag on demand.
Also, the U.S. stock market has remained buoyant despite the March rate hike, another factor, known as the "wealth effect," that may sustain strong consumer spending.

However, the source said the Fed was prepared to gauge to what extent possible structural changes in the U.S. economy are accounting for the current departure from the historical demand/inflation pattern that would have previously warranted a clearly tighter policy stance.
"The rapid growth in the workforce is a factor that may help, but that can go only so far," the source said. "There is a point where you'll be racking the bottom."
As tight labor markets lured discouraged workers back into the workplace, a factor dampening wage gains, the workforce has been growing at a faster rate than demographics would suggest.

Another factor that may allow for trend growth to be as high as 3.0 percent is the fact that productivity -- mainly in the service sector where gains are most difficult to measure -- may be understated after years of U.S. companies pouring billions of dollars into new technology.
"Productivity is probably understated and we may be looking at an economy that can grow faster than previously thought without generating inflation, but up to a point," the source acknowledged.
Another Fed source noted that the broad measure of unemployment, or U-6, has fallen to 9.0 percent from 12.0 percent in 1994.
This indicated that employers will be able to draw only so much more from the pool of available workers until competitive wage pressures emerge.

"There is no doubt there is a lot of pressure on resource utilization," the second source said, noting that the Fed has been carefully monitoring labor markets since the unemployment rate began to trend below 5.5 percent in the summer of 1996.
"The pace of growth for all of 1997 cannot remain as high as the pace of growth in the first quarter," the source said.
The source added that the Fed is expecting the economy to slow by itself in the course of the year or that it would adjust its policy to ensure it will slow.
"Is 5.0 percent, let's say, sustainable, trend growth? The answer is no," the source said.
